svg.title: 2. Direct Connect, VPN backup and routing
svg.text: AWS to on-prem: steer with local-preference communities
On-prem to AWS: prefer DX, VPN as last resort
Inside the Transit Gateway: same destination, which route wins?
Failure modes this design was tested against (game day, quarterly)
Routing and failover: four transit VIFs, BGP communities, BFD, and a VPN that only wins when DX is gone
All DX down: the same three
DC A routers send 10.0.0.0/11 with 7224:7300 (high) on VIFs 1 and 2.
DC B routers send 10.32.0.0/11 with 7224:7300 (high) on VIFs 3 and 4.
Every router also sends the other site's /11 and the 10.0.0.0/10 summary with 7224:7100 (low).
Result: AWS uses the location next to the data that owns the prefix, ECMP across its two VIFs,
and moves to the other location (then across the DCI) only when the first one is gone.
AWS evaluates these communities before AS_PATH length, so they are the reliable lever.
AWS advertises only the allowed prefixes, 10.64.0.0/12 and 10.80.0.0/12, on every VIF.
The VPN advertises the same two, because the onprem TGW route table holds only static summaries.
Edge routers set local-pref 200 on DX-learned routes and 100 on VPN-learned routes.
On-prem advertises 6 prefixes per VIF. The default limit is 100, and going over it drops
the BGP session. Prefix controls can raise the allocation to 1,000.
1. The most specific prefix, always first
7. VPN over private DX, then Site-to-Site VPN routes
The trap: a 10.0.12.0/22 learned over VPN
longest match comes before attachment type.

alarm when the onprem route table has

The other VIF at the same location (ECMP)

Site-to-Site VPN, 4 tunnels, ECMP on the TGW
A link, with BFD missing on the router
Nothing. Traffic is black-holed until the hold timer expires
